## Install

Nothing here is code-signed yet, so your system will ask you to confirm the first time.

| | File | First time |
|---|---|---|
| **Windows** | `BoardDock-3.0.0-win-x64-setup.exe` (installer) or `…-portable.exe` (no install) | Choose **More info → Run anyway**. |
| **macOS** | `BoardDock-3.0.0-mac-….dmg` (open it and drag BoardDock into Applications) | Right-click the app and choose **Open**. |
| **Linux** | `BoardDock-3.0.0-linux-x86_64.AppImage` (`chmod +x` it, then run it) or the `.deb` (`sudo apt install ./BoardDock-3.0.0-linux-….deb`) | Nothing. |
| **In your browser** | [danmover.github.io/boarddock](https://danmover.github.io/boarddock) | Nothing is uploaded: it all runs in your browser. |

The desktop app does two things the browser can't: it opens Cadence Allegro `.brd` boards (with KiCad 10 or newer installed, free from kicad.org), and **Open plate** hands a plate to a slicer you have installed.

**Nothing BoardDock makes has been printed and tried yet.** Print the test-fit kit first (30 to 40 minutes), and treat anything about fit, strength and clips as coming from the model and its checks, not from a real print.

This is the first release since v0.2.0 (a v2.1.0 was prepared but never published), so everything below is new since v0.2.0.

## What's new

### Connectors
- **Far more connectors are recognised on imported boards**, above all as Allegro libraries name them: IPC-7251 header names, a maker's name in front of the part number, part numbers with the dashes taken out, upper case, `_10P` pin counts. Checked against KiCad's whole connector library, 94 % of its footprints are identified (98 % leaving out bare solder pads), and none of its 5,600 other parts are taken for a connector. A chip or diode with only a connector-like word in its name (a diode package called SMA, a TRS3232, a USB4640) stays a chip.
- **New connector families**: board-to-board (Samtec, Hirose, Molex SlimStack), M.2, mini PCIe, PCIe and DIMM sockets (the holder keeps clear of the card in them), XLR, banana jacks, M12 and M8, TOSLINK, SIM slots, SATA, SFP cages, mini-DIN, IEC C14 inlets, MMCX, MCX and SMB, the 20-pin Cortex debug connector, and many more makers' terminal blocks, headers, USB, RJ45, D-sub and DC jacks. Each is wired as what it is (an SFP cage is a network port, a C14 inlet takes a kettle-type lead, TOSLINK goes only to TOSLINK).
- **Sizes checked against KiCad's library** (drawn from the makers' datasheets) for SATA, XLR, banana, BNC, SMA, TOSLINK, SIM, SFP, SO-DIMM, mini PCIe, the mezzanine bodies, the 3.5 mm jack and the right-angle box header.
- **Every connector is in the toolbox**, with its own picture, and drawn as itself in 3D: round SMA, XLR, M12 and mini-DIN barrels, a figure-8 mains socket, pin sockets with visible holes, blue relays.

### Adding boards and parts yourself
- **`boards/`**: put a board's files (KiCad, Eagle, ODB++, IPC-2581, Gerber…) in `boards/<name>/` with a small `board.json`, run `npm run boards`, and it shows in the app's library as a community board. The report says which connectors it couldn't identify.
- **`parts/`**: teach BoardDock a connector's part numbers with one line of JSON, or add a new part type (size, plug, what it connects to, and a look made of simple shapes). It appears in the toolbox under Contributed.
- Both come with step-by-step instructions an AI can follow (`boards/AGENTS.md`, `parts/AGENTS.md`), a check on every pull request, and an optional Claude job that does the work when a `boards` or `parts` label is added (it needs the repository's `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` secret).

### J-Links and USB-serial adapters
- **J-Links and adapters are ordinary boards**, docked and cabled like any board. Small boards stack in columns on their long edge, one release rod down the whole column.
- **One press adds what's missing**: "Add 3 J-Links + 2 adapters" gives each debug header a J-Link with the right connector (10-pin, 20-pin Cortex or JTAG box) and each UART header an adapter, docked beside their board.
- **Debug and serial panel** on Plugs: every header, its probe, ribbon length (one click to fix a short one), dock slot and pin 1. A printable **bench sheet** has it all on one page.
- A female header used for UART gets male-ended jumpers (drawn and bought that way); guessed UART pin names say to check yours.
- The column holders' pegs and holes now print without supports.

### Wiring and power
- **PoE**: a PoE switch, and a "PoE HAT fitted" option; a board on a PoE port needs no supply, within the switch's budget.
- **Arduino DC jacks** only take a pack in their range (7 to 12 V); Auto-connect picks the one nearest 9 V, and the advice offers a 9 V pack when none fits.
- **"Add a USB hub"** is sized to what needs plugging in, and says what goes to your computer.
- **Cables to buy** use the same wording and lengths everywhere, with an option to buy every Ethernet lead at one length. Each cable Auto-connect made says why.
- Plug packs no longer get a printed holder in the loose layout.

### Auto-arrange and cable routing
- **Auto-arrange plans for the cables**: it tries layouts, scores each on cable length, crossings, cables under rails, blocked plugs and rail used, and checks the best with the real router. On 13 test racks: 23 % less cable, the longest cable 24 % shorter, crossings from 87 to 18 (rails are about a third longer on the balanced goal; the Compact goal turns that round).
- **Auto-arrange options**: probes beside their board and stacked, a goal (balanced, compact, short cables, easy to reach), like boards grouped, mains at one end, hosts near devices, room to grow, back-to-back pairing, stock cable lengths, hot boards apart, fewest printed parts. **Pack new boards only** leaves the rest of the rack where it is.
- **Smarter routing**: crossings under the rails spread out and pinned, cables kept off each other, rails, stands and plugs, combs wherever cables cross a stand, tags on clear spots. On the 144 test racks the collision check went from 458 to about 35 mm³.
- **Debug ribbons and jumpers never block taking a holder off**: over another board's dock they rise clear of its lift-off and release lever, or go round the end.
- **Plug packs on the rack's powerboard** have their lead drawn from the outlet and checked against its length.
- **Cables: off**, for when you only want holders and plug covers: no cables, combs or cable shopping, and a simple port list for cradles and caps. Your cables come back when you switch it on.

### Layout
- **Cluster preset** on Start: a Pi 4 or Pi 5 cluster with switch, powerboard and supplies (or PoE) in one go.
- **Complete this rack**: supplies, outlets, a switch and an uplink, in one undo step.
- **Layout lock**: lock the layout, a rail or a dock; automatic changes leave it alone, and each writes a receipt you can undo.
- **Copy to…**: copy a board's holder options and port settings to other boards.
- Back-to-back pairing works by touch; dock labels say how each dock stands.

### The 3D view
- **Cables are translucent**, coloured by kind (colour-blind safe, with a key), with a bright rim and core; the one you pick stands out.
- **Power runs through them**: glowing streaks move from each supply to its board, now on PoE, mains and leads that leave the rack too, and boards on PoE or a plug pack light up.
- **Isolate and X-ray** the selection, **What's new** tinted in 3D, **mains zones** shaded (and a Check line when mains sits close to a low-voltage board), a typed **rotation** box with 15°, 45° and 90° snaps.
- **Command palette** (Ctrl/Cmd+K, or the search button on a phone).
- Labels group per holder, stay on top, and show only for real leads; the camera frames the whole row.

### Printing and export
- **Slice and download all G-code** from the main button once your start code is known; Download everything can include it.
- Start code you paste for any printer is checked (bed size, moves off the bed, temperatures, other printers' commands) before it's used.
- Parts on a plate are always far enough apart for two brims; the print settings describe the skirt the slicer lays.
- The thin-gap print check catches gaps by width, so a 0.09 mm print-in-place gap is flagged.
- A **buy, print and tools checklist** you tick as you go, saved in the project.

### Also
- Several files imported at once stay on Start with a Check the boards button; adding to a built rack says where each board went; Steps can play **only what's new**.
- Check items say "OK to print" or "worth a look", with a fix button where there is one.
- A layout you've built before comes back instantly, and a slow build shows what it's working on.

## Known limits

- The peg fit, crush ribs, the long release rod through a column, the slot for a board nothing clips in, and the tongue under a tall column are all untested in plastic.
- A second J-Link for one board needs a ribbon of about 250 mm (a 30 cm ribbon; the Debug panel says so).
- Big racks are slow to build the first time.
- Some connector sizes are still typical ones, with no public datasheet drawing to check them against: M.2 sockets, PCIe slot depth, full-size DIMM, M12, RCA, DisplayPort, mini HDMI and Qwiic, and every connector's plug.
- Two boards that mate on a board-to-board connector aren't treated as one stack: put them in a stack by hand.
- Allegro `.brd` import was tested with a stand-in for KiCad's tool, not yet with a real Allegro board.
